item.title: A friendship that blossoms in the Mu Us Desert
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-24
A friendship that blossoms in the Mu Us Desert A group photo from the 1999 donation ceremony, where Ronald Sakolsky presents $5,000 for afforestation efforts, is preserved by Bai Fan. (Photo: Courtesy of Luoyang No. 2 Foreign Language School) In Pennsylvania, the United States, the Allegheny River winds through Pittsburgh. Just east of the city lies the township of Plum, where Ronald Sakolsky, known to his Chinese friends as "Sai Kaosi," has called home for many years. "Part of my heart is still in China." Upon returning recently from a trip across the Pacific, Sakolsky found it difficult to hide how deeply he missed the country. His living room is filled with mementos from his travels. The sofa is covered with photos he brought back from his trip. But his most treasured keepsake is a large cross-stitch embroidery presented to him by Yin Yuzhen. Green leaves symbolizing peace surround a globe, with China and the United States stitched in different colors. The Chinese characters meaning "one earth, one dream" capture the deep friendship that has grown between Sakolsky and Yin over more than two decades. "Yuanfen" -- a special bond or sense of destiny -- is the word Sakolsky repeatedly uses in Chinese when talking about his story with China. "It's all yuanfen," he said. Ronald Sakolsky poses for a picture with Yin Yuzhen and her husband in front of a tree they planted together in 2000 in Erdos, north China's Inner Mongolia autonomous region, Aug. 24. (Photo/Zeng Yue) In 1999, at the age of 40, Sakolsky was a history teacher at a middle school in Pennsylvania. By chance, he came to Luoyang, central China's Henan province, to teach through a China-U.S. teacher exchange program. One day in October that year, he turned on the television as usual to watch the news. On the screen was a vast stretch of desert, where a petite Chinese woman from a rural area was carrying a bundle of tree saplings taller than she was. And that woman was Yin Yuzhen. "I suddenly burst into tears," he recalled. Deeply moved by what he saw, he thought, "I have to do something." For the next two months, Sakolsky searched everywhere for a way to make a donation. Eventually, he found a charitable organization willing to provide $5,000 with no conditions attached. Sakolsky insisted that every cent of the money go toward helping Yin plant trees. In the spring of 2000, Sakolsky traveled to the Mu Us Desert in the Inner Mongolia autonomous region in north China. As he watched Yin plant the frail-looking saplings, he could not help wondering: Could a desert really be turned into a forest? It seemed impossible. The second day after returning to China in August this year, he stood in the forest that had been planted with the $5,000 donation. Yin had named it "Sai Kaosi Forest." Ronald Sakolsky takes care of two green plants he has planted in his front yard, with the national flags of China and the United States hanging beside them, Sept. 11. (People's Daily/Li Zhiwei) The dream he had once thought impossible had become a reality. More than 50,000 trees now grow there, forming a vast forest. At the airport, he and Yin embraced in tears after 26 years apart. The following day, they planted another evergreen tree together as a symbol of their friendship. "I have hugged Americans, and I have hugged Chinese. The feeling is the same," Sakolsky said repeatedly after his latest trip to China. Since returning home, he has been sharing his experiences online and reconnecting with old friends. Last week, he spoke to about 50 neighbors in his community, and soon he plans to address nearly 1,000 residents in Pittsburgh. "We've sparked a flame of people-to-people exchange. Now, we just need to keep it burning," he said. He picked up a photo taken during his trip to China, showing him and Yin leaning against each other's shoulders and embracing in tears. "If I had to choose one photo to represent the friendship between the American and Chinese people, it would be this one," he said. "This photo tells the whole story. It captures everything about this friendship." "The American and Chinese people share the same basic human goodness. Both have kindness in their hearts," Sakolsky said. Photo shows the family forest farm of Yin Yuzhen, located in the Mu Us Desert in Wushen banner, Erdos, north China's Inner Mongolia autonomous region. (Photo courtesy of the publicity department of Wushen banner) In his view, Chinese and Americans both love their families, hope their children can have better lives, cherish peace and want to make the land beneath their feet a better place. These shared values matter far more than the differences brought about by nationality, he said. They form the simplest and most genuine foundation for people-to-people exchanges between China and the United States. Outside the window, two newly planted green plants stand side by side on the lawn in front of Sakolsky's, with the national flags of China and the United States fluttering nearby. He said he had deliberately planted the two flowers in the front yard as a symbol of his hopes for friendship, peace and the protection of the shared planet. "People-to-people friendship works. Our story will continue, just like the forest in the Mu Us Desert thousands of miles away, growing year after year," Sakolsky said. Stories of people coming to know and understand one another will continue to cross the ocean, putting down new rings of growth, one after another. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. item.title: 'We remain committed to China, continue to invest for the long term': Amway CEO
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-24
'We remain committed to China, continue to invest for the long term': Amway CEO "Over the past 30 years in China, one lesson has stood out: lasting success is built on trust, mutual respect, and strong relationships." President and CEO of Amway Michael Nelson recently gave an interview to People's Daily, prior to Chinese President Xi Jinping's state visit to the United States. Nelson emphasized that when businesses prioritize value creation and meaningful connections, they foster deeper understanding, trust, and shared prosperity. Those are outcomes that benefit not only individual companies but also communities, countries, and the broader global economy as well, he noted. Since entering China over three decades ago, Amway has witnessed the country's rapid economic ascent and the profound transformation of its consumer landscape. "China has evolved from an important growth market into one of our most strategic markets," Nelson told People's Daily. He stressed that Amway's relationship with China has always been anchored in a long-term perspective, sustained investment, and a shared commitment to creating value. "What gives me confidence is not just the scale of opportunity, but the foundation we've built over thirty years. We remain fully committed to China, and we will continue to invest for the long term," he said. Nelson highlighted four guiding principles for Amway's journey in China: commitment, shared success, local innovation, and sustainable growth. The company first invested in China in 1992, breaking ground on a manufacturing facility in Guangzhou's development zone. That Guangzhou base has grown into Amway's largest production hub worldwide and the only facility capable of manufacturing its entire product portfolio. It supplies more than 50 global markets and accounts for 55 percent of Amway's total global output value. To date, Amway has completed 10 rounds of capital investment in China, establishing a fully localized value chain that spans research and development, manufacturing, retail, consumer engagement, and after-sales services, laying a solid foundation for local development. "These investments reflect our confidence in China's economic resilience and our enduring commitment to supporting the country's long-term health, growth, and innovation," Nelson noted. "China's dynamic business environment and collaborative spirit have consistently created opportunities for mutual success," Nelson noted, adding that local innovation is a key reason the company has been able to grow and adapt over time. "China's strong technological capabilities, entrepreneurial energy, and rapidly evolving consumer preferences continue to shape how we innovate, serve consumers, and evolve our business model. We view China not only as a major market, but as a vital innovation center that informs our global strategy," Nelson said. Many of the ideas, insights, and capabilities developed here are helping shape the company's future and strengthen its ability to meet the changing needs of consumers, he added. Earlier this year, Nelson attended the China Development Forum 2026, where he had in-depth communication with business representatives around the world on China's 15th Five-Year Plan, opening-up, as well as global cooperation. He said one aspect of the 15th Five-Year Plan that is especially relevant to Amway is the continued focus on building a Healthy China. He sees strong alignment among relevant policies, the Chinese government's emphasis on innovation, the constantly upgrading consumption, and Amway's mission. "That alignment gives us confidence to continue investing in China," Nelson said. According to him, Amway will grow its business by investing in healthcare, innovation, digital infrastructure, and supply chain optimization. The company is continuing to invest in local talent, partnerships, and capabilities, so as to provide solid support for its development in China and share more opportunities with the country, Nelson said. As a business leader, he places high value on strategic foresight -- a quality he finds reflected in China's long-term planning. "China's structured approach to development provides the stability companies need to confidently invest in the capabilities required to serve today's consumers and prepare for tomorrow's challenges," he said. He said Amway China aims at long-term growth, and follows a clear vision for development and a stable framework that supports investment and innovation. "We have always believed that meaningful success is built through consistency, patience, and a willingness to continue investing through change," he told People's Daily. Projects such as the development of an Amway-owned farm in Pengzhou, southwest China's Sichuan province, represent a deeper commitment to organic farming practices, botanical excellence, and a vertical supply chain. They reflect the company's determination to continue building a foundation that can support sustainable growth for decades to come. "Every trip to China reinforces what has impressed me for many years: the energy, optimism, and commitment people bring to building better lives for themselves, their families, and their communities," he said. These shared spirits of people foster deep connections that transcend national and cultural boundaries. Nelson is optimistic about the development of China-U.S. relations, believing the two sides can accomplish big things when they work together. "Looking ahead, my hope is that there continue to be opportunities for people of the two countries to learn from one another, build relationships, and work together toward common goals," he said. item.title: Young Chinese find roots, inspiration in Long March legacy
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-24
Young Chinese find roots, inspiration in Long March legacy GUIYANG, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- On stage, Red Army soldiers on the Long March braved raging rivers, snow-covered mountains and vast grasslands. Some fell amid a hail of gunfire, while others marched on to the end. When the performance ended and the lights came up, 24-year-old actor Tian Hongqiang found himself back in the present, witnessing a new China for all those who had sacrificed their lives. "I saw a glimmer of light shining in the audience's eyes. Grey-haired elders and young students in school uniforms gave us their thumbs-up," Tian said. "That makes me feel the power of the spirit we are trying to convey." For over two years, Tian has performed in "The Great Turning Point," a large-scale immersive production about the Long March being staged in Zunyi, southwest China's Guizhou Province. Known as China's "city of historic turning point," Zunyi holds a special place in the nation's history. In January 1935, during the Long March, the Communist Party of China (CPC) convened the Zunyi Meeting in a two-story building here at a critical historical crossroads. In October 1934, the CPC was forced to retreat from the Central Soviet Area in east China's Jiangxi and move northwest after enduring a series of encirclement campaigns by rival forces of the Kuomintang party (KMT). The setback was the result of left-leaning errors in military strategy and rigid Soviet-inspired dogmatism. The CPC-led Red Army fought its way across the Xiangjiang River in Guangxi and broke through the KMT troops' blockade, but suffered tens of thousands of casualties in the battle. The three-day meeting was thus convened to draw lessons. In the end, many key issues were resolved, including the establishment of a new Party leadership with Mao Zedong at the helm. Today, Zunyi is one of China's best-known destinations for historical education tours, which take visitors to sites associated with the country's revolutionary history. This year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March. In Zunyi, the history that once unfolded in meeting rooms, mountain passes and battlefields is being retold via theater, immersive experiences and cultural products, drawing younger generations closer to the historical events. "The Great Turning Point," centered on the history of the Zunyi Meeting, premiered on Jan. 15, 2024, the meeting's 89th anniversary, and has staged more than 2,500 performances so far. Wang Liming, a marketing executive with the company behind the production, said about 60 percent of its audience are 25 to 50 years old, with many parents joining their children to watch. "We hope to help young people develop an emotional connection with this history, so that it is no longer just words and pictures in a textbook," Wang said. Among the audience was 10-year-old Xu Chen'en, who traveled from Chongqing Municipality in southwest China with her mother, Chen Jinghong. "I think the Red Army soldiers were very brave," Xu said. "We should learn from them and face our own difficulties courageously." Her mother sees the experience as a form of education that sinks in over time. "It is like planting a seed in her heart," Chen said. "She can experience the culture of the Long March now and gradually come to understand it as she grows up." For another visitor, surnamed Xia, the performance became an experience shared by three generations. She watched it with her 56-year-old aunt and 85-year-old grandmother. "My grandmother's generation has a strong emotional bond with this history, and she was deeply moved," Xia said. "For us, theater makes it much more immersive." The family's next stop was Loushan Pass, north of Zunyi, another landmark on the Long March route. After the Zunyi Meeting, the Red Army achieved a major victory there. What was once a battlefield is now a popular tourism destination. Twice a day, a live-action performance lasting nearly an hour recreates battle scenes. Roughly 90 performers are residents of nearby villages. "We want to make the spirit of the Long March something visitors can see and experience," said Zhu Jingbo, a local culture and tourism official. Visitors can take part in the performance, playing roles as local residents, helping to transport supplies and tending to wounded soldiers. Zhu said creators consulted historians while developing the show, including firsthand accounts of locals guiding Red Army troops across the region. This approach, he said, is intended to move beyond static museum displays, make revolutionary history more accessible to younger visitors, and create new opportunities for local communities. Around 15,000 students visit the Loushan Pass area each year on educational trips. Villagers who take part in performances can earn an additional 2,000 to 3,000 yuan (approximately 298 to 447 U.S. dollars) a month, depending on their roles. Such immersive experiences are part of a wider shift in China's revolutionary education tours. In recent years, historical education tours have increasingly diversified, with performances, study tours and cultural products complementing traditional visits to memorials and historic sites. China's plan for building the country into a tourism powerhouse during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) also calls for further exploring the historical and contemporary value of revolutionary heritage, improving exhibitions at revolutionary tourism sites, and expanding cultural products and performances. Thus the creative reinterpretation of the Long March spirit stretches far beyond museums and scenic spots. Zunyi's bustling downtown Red Army Street boasts a full range of Long March-themed cultural products, including figurines, backpacks and custom cups, making revolutionary culture accessible to younger audiences. Near the historical site of the Zunyi Meeting, designer Han Bing sells small Red Army figurines. He said many of his customers are students, particularly from primary and middle schools, while older visitors often buy the figurines as gifts for children. The shop, which opened in 2019, has maintained brisk business, with daily sales sometimes exceeding 12,000 yuan. For Han, the connection with the Long March is personal. He comes from Liping County in Guizhou, the first county seat reached by the Central Red Army after entering the province. Han grew up hearing a family story about a wooden bridge across the Bazhou River that Red Army troops once crossed. His great-grandfather, he said, helped build the bridge, which later became known locally as the "Red Army Bridge." Influenced by his family, Han developed an interest in revolutionary history at an early age and later studied art. Growing up during the early decades of China's reform and opening-up, he said he was initially fascinated by cultures from abroad. But when he started his own business and began exploring Chinese history and revolutionary culture more deeply, he felt as though he had found his roots. "I wanted to share that feeling with other people," Han said. "So I turned images of Red Army soldiers into figurines, using a form that younger people can relate to." When asked why the Long March should still be remembered 90 years later, he answered with a story from his own life. At the most difficult point in his entrepreneurial journey, Han said he had lost nearly all the money he had invested. Alone, he went to the top of Loushan Pass and recited a poem written there by Mao Zedong. "Fear not the strong pass iron-clad on all sides! The summit's now surmounted with big strides..." As he recited, he said his determination gradually returned. "What inspires me most is the enduring optimism of the Long March, the sense that hope never dies," Han said. "It's an inexhaustible source of strength." Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: China secures bumper harvest with stable fertilizer supply, smart farming
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-24
China secures bumper harvest with stable fertilizer supply, smart farming WUHAN/HARBIN, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- As combine harvesters bring the autumn harvest to a close across central China's Hubei Province, local farmer Fu Pengcheng is preparing his 1,000 mu (66.7 hectares) of farmland for winter wheat rotation, reassured by stable fertilizer supplies heading into the upcoming planting season. The 42-year-old farmer has stockpiled 40 tonnes of fertilizer at 3,065 yuan (454.29 U.S. dollars) per tonne. "Though slightly higher compared with last year, the price is still reasonable," said Fu, adding that his county has ample fertilizer stocks for him to replenish at any time. Like Fu, farmers across China today no longer have to scramble for fertilizer or stockpile it during the busy farming season, nor do they have to worry about fertilizer price spikes. Against tightening global fertilizer supply rattled by geopolitical headwinds, the country's targeted measures have secured agricultural supplies and underpinned national food security. China's grain production has stayed on firm footing this year. Official data released in July put summer grain output at 150.7 billion kilograms, up 0.7 percent year on year, marking the first time the harvest has topped 150 billion kilograms. The country is on track to meet its annual grain output target of around 700 billion kilograms. An aerial drone photo shows a harvester operating in a paddy field in Dufan Village of Dawu County, central China's Hubei Province, Sept. 15, 2026. (Xinhua/Du Zixuan) STABLE FERTILIZER SUPPLY Fertilizer, an essential input for grain farming, faces severe global supply strains in 2026. Escalating geopolitical tensions in the Gulf region have disrupted vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical export route for fertilizers. The disruption has severely fragmented global fertilizer supply chains. The World Bank forecasts a 31 percent overall surge in global fertilizer prices for 2026. Most economies are grappling with fertilizer shortages and soaring farming costs, which pose growing threats to their food security. As the world's major fertilizer producer and consumer, China has rolled out targeted measures to counter global market volatility, stabilize domestic fertilizer supply and underpin food security against external challenges. Early this year, China's top economic regulator issued a guideline to ensure year-round fertilizer supply and price stability for spring plowing, requiring multiple departments to coordinate efforts to boost fertilizer production, cut farming costs, optimize reserve management and promote scientific fertilization practices. Across the country, fertilizer producers have responded by expanding output and diversifying procurement. This photo taken on July 25, 2026 shows a smart fertilizer warehouse at Hubei Yihua Phosphorus Chemical Co., Ltd. in Yichang, central China's Hubei Province. (Xinhua) At the production park of Hubei Yihua Group Co., Ltd. in Yichang, Hubei Province, intelligent production lines are running at full speed. Bags of fertilizer are automatically filled, sealed and palletized before being quickly transferred to the finished product warehouse through an intelligent loading system. Faced with sharp price increases and supply fluctuations of fertilizer raw materials such as sulfur, the company has actively expanded diversified overseas procurement channels to stabilize external import sources. It has also deepened cooperation with major central state-owned enterprises such as Sinopec and PetroChina, signing long-term raw material procurement agreements to lock in preferential procurement terms and supply quotas. In the first eight months of this year, the company's total domestic fertilizer output reached 2.95 million tonnes. Beyond corporate efforts, China's systematic reserve and distribution network forms the backbone of fertilizer supply security. The country has a commercial fertilizer reserve system, with a full-spectrum reserve framework covering nitrogen, phosphorus, compound, potash and disaster-relief fertilizers across major agricultural provinces, said Ye Xingqing, a researcher with the Development Research Center of the State Council. A nationwide agricultural supply network further ensures efficient distribution, with over 4,800 agricultural input enterprises and 280,000 grassroots service outlets across rural areas. During this year's spring plowing season, China released more than 10 million tonnes of state commercial fertilizer reserves, strongly supporting stable grain production. An aerial drone photo taken on July 29, 2026 shows an agricultural plane carrying out aerial crop protection operations over a corn field of Beidahuang Group in northeast China's Heilongjiang Province. (Photo by Ren Baoji/Xinhua) Thanks to coordinated policy regulation, expanded industrial output and industry self-discipline, domestic fertilizer prices have stayed largely stable this year, in stark contrast to sharp global price hikes driven by geopolitical conflicts, said Wang Xiaoxue, an official with the China Agricultural Means of Production Association. SMART FARMING TECHNOLOGY Complementing stable material supplies, advanced agricultural technology has helped China mitigate the impact of natural disasters and lift grain yields, helping secure a resilient autumn harvest. Henan, a key grain-producing province in central China, has leveraged drone monitoring and smart field management to improve disaster response after Typhoon Dolphin struck in August. Rather than sending teams to inspect fields on foot, researchers use surveillance drones to send real-time soil and waterlogging data to smart platforms. This allows fast drainage and targeted loss control. Wang Qiang, an associate professor at Henan Agricultural University, led the practice at an agricultural demonstration park, deploying drones to assess damage instead of wading into fields. His smart farm project in Luohe City of Henan, uses patrol drones to stream real-time field data to a smart management platform. "We spot waterlogged areas and activate drainage promptly to curb losses," Wang said. He added that agricultural demonstration sites nationwide let farmers test new technologies on the ground. These projects speed up the upgrade of China's farm machinery fleet and make it smarter. A farmer operates an agricultural machine equipped with BeiDou Navigation Satellite System (BDS) in a soybean field in northeast China's Heilongjiang Province, June 13, 2026. (Photo by Qian Boyu/Xinhua) The province has achieved a 90-percent comprehensive mechanization rate for crop planting and harvesting, with wheat and corn production fully mechanized. Nationwide, BeiDou-guided autonomous tractors, intelligent seeders, automated water-fertilizer irrigation systems and straw balers now cover the entire planting, management and harvesting cycle, powering precision farming. In Heilongjiang, China's largest grain-producing province, autumn harvesting is underway. Its overall farm planting and harvesting mechanization rate has led the country for years, surpassing 99 percent. Widely seen as a cornerstone of national food security, the province is rolling out new technology to boost per-hectare yields and crop quality. The province deployed over 25,000 precision seeders and 33,000 crop-protection drones this year to lift farm operation standards and efficiency, said Zhu Huasheng, deputy director of the provincial agriculture and rural affairs department. Official figures also show Heilongjiang has dispatched more than 26,000 agricultural officials and experts to the fields so far this year, guiding farmers to adopt new technologies. Cheng Guoqiang, dean of the National School of Food Security Strategy at Renmin University of China, said that in a year of tightening global grain supplies, China's steady grain production has helped stabilize global market expectations. item.title: Harnessing collective strength for shared development and a brighter future for humanity
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-24
Harnessing collective strength for shared development and a brighter future for humanity Development is a timeless theme for humanity, and the master key to solving all problems facing the world. On Sept. 21, 2021, Chinese President Xi Jinping put forward the Global Development Initiative (GDI) at the general debate of the 76th session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA). Designed as a comprehensive framework to tackle pressing development obstacles, the GDI offers a Chinese perspective that balances pragmatic action with a commitment to shared prosperity. Over the past five years, China has remained committed to advancing the GDI, collaborating with international partners to translate its vision into concrete results and injecting renewed momentum into global development amid growing uncertainty. Rising geopolitical tensions, the resurgence of unilateral policies, and a sluggish global economic recovery have exacerbated existing imbalances, governance gaps, and inequities. The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) Report 2026, released by the United Nations recently, shows that of the 139 SDG targets with available trend data, only 36 percent are on track or making moderate progress; nearly half are advancing too slowly; and 15 percent have actually regressed. Global development is facing serious challenges. The GDI responds directly to these systemic challenges by addressing structural gaps in global development governance. Grounded in six core principles -- development as a priority, a people-centered approach, inclusive development that benefits all, innovation-driven development, harmony between man and nature, and results-oriented actions -- it has broadened the practical pathways for sustainable progress and deepened the architecture of global development cooperation. Rather than treating development resources as tools for political leverage or strategic competition, the GDI has always been guided by the common well-being of humanity. It recognizes varying national development stages, needs, and sovereign rights, offering robust support to developing countries as they pursue independent, equitable, and sustainable growth. Since its launch, the GDI has steadily expanded its network of partners and grown in international relevance. China has held high-level meetings on the GDI during four consecutive UNGA sessions and launched the Forum on Global Action for Shared Development to strengthen policy dialogue and exchanges of ideas. More than 130 countries and international organizations have expressed support for the GDI and participated in its cooperation, and 88 countries have joined the Group of Friends of the GDI. The U.N. Task Force on Leveraging Partnerships Toward the Implementation of the 2030 Agenda has attracted the participation of more than 20 development agencies. To complement these efforts, China has launched more than 30 cooperation mechanisms and platforms. Through the China-U.N. Peace and Development Fund, the Global Development and South-South Cooperation Fund, and other funding initiatives, more than US$23 billion have been mobilized. Over 2,000 cooperation projects have been launched under joint efforts, providing training for more than 200,000 people in different professions. This has offered strong support for Global South countries to enhance their development capability. The GDI is a practical platform for international cooperation that brings hope, opportunities and sustainable development to millions of people, said Kenyan Ambassador to China Willy Kipkorir Bett. Over the past five years, people-centered cooperation projects have been launched across the world, bringing tangible benefits to ordinary people in more than 120 countries, and making the gains of common development tangible and accessible. In Nigeria, a China-aided Juncao technology demonstration farm has helped boost grain production and has been hailed by the local government as a model project for ensuring food security. In Grenada, Chinese agricultural specialists have conducted field training on advanced cultivation methods, enabling farmers to improve crop quality, stabilize incomes, and modernize niche agricultural sectors. Meanwhile, Laos's Monsoon Wind Power Project has commenced operations, generating over 1,000 permanent jobs, cutting annual carbon emissions by 1.56 million tons, and advancing the country's transition toward green, low-carbon energy systems. Parallel to infrastructure and agricultural initiatives, China has established capacity-building platforms such as the China House of Foreign-Aid Programs Trainee and the Youth Leaders' Community for Global Development. These programs are nurturing a new generation of development professionals and engaging youth in sustainability efforts, ensuring long-term momentum for shared global progress. As an important global public good provided by China to the international community, the fundamental logic of the GDI is to make the pie bigger rather than divide it up, and to empower all for win-win outcomes rather than engage in zero-sum competition. This stands in fundamental contrast to the exclusionary logic underlying the so-called "China squeeze" narrative promoted by some Western institutions and media. Global development cooperation is currently at a critical stage of shifting its sources of momentum and adjusting its structure. Revitalizing global development requires countries to build greater solidarity and pool their strength to address imbalances in development. It also calls for practicing true multilateralism and improving the global governance system. As a new round of scientific and technological revolution, including artificial intelligence, accelerates, all countries need to uphold openness and inclusiveness, learn from one another and draw on each other's strengths, break down technological barriers and barriers to cooperation, and ensure that every country can keep pace with the times. Looking ahead, China will continue to fulfill its role as a responsible major country, deepen all-round international development cooperation, and work with countries around the world with unity and determination to advance the implementation of the GDI, improve global development governance, and jointly illuminate a brighter future of prosperity and progress for humanity. item.title: Xi says China, U.S. should be partners, not rivals
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-24
Home>>
Xi says China, U.S. should be partners, not rivals (Xinhua) 08:58, September 24, 2026
WASHINGTON, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- China and the United States should be partners, not rivals, Chinese President Xi Jinping said on Wednesday. China and the United States are both great countries, and the two peoples are both great peoples, Xi said in a written speech upon his arrival for a U.S. state visit. Noting that the two peoples have maintained friendly exchanges for a long time and their interests are deeply intertwined, he said that the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand, complement each other and benefit the world. (Web editor: Zhang Kaiwei, Liang Jun)

(Xinhua/Zhang Tao) BEIJING, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- People across China on Wednesday held various activities to celebrate the ninth Chinese farmers' harvest festival. The festival is the first national festival created specifically for the country's farmers. This year's festival falls on Wednesday. item.title: Follow Xi | 'The hope of the China-U.S. relationship lies in the people'
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-24
Follow Xi | 'The hope of the China-U.S. relationship lies in the people'
"Though geographically far apart, our peoples boast a long history of friendly exchanges," Chinese President Xi Jinping said at the Welcoming Dinner hosted by Local Governments and Friendly Organizations in the United States on Sep. 22, 2015. Over the years, Xi has attached great importance to and personally promoted people-to-people exchanges between China and the U.S., sharing stories of friendship between the two peoples on many occasions. In 1985, Xi, then Party chief of Zhengding county in north China's Hebei Province, led a delegation to Iowa, known as the "granary and breadbasket of America," to study agriculture and animal husbandry. A sincere friendship began there, spanning four decades and growing stronger with time. A century ago, Kuliang in Fuzhou, southeast China's Fujian Province became a place where people from China and the U.S. forged a warm bond of friendship and mutual understanding. Over the years, the "Kuliang Friends" have continued to carry this friendship across borders. During World War II, members of the American Flying Tigers traveled across the ocean to fight alongside the Chinese people. Today, this precious historical memory continues to be cherished and passed down by their descendants. In 1971, the U.S. table tennis team visited Beijing, becoming the first delegation of Americans to visit China in decades. It gave rise to the famous phrase "a little ball moves the big ball." Ping-Pong Diplomacy broke the ice between two nations and reopened a door that would go on to reshape the world. One moving story after another has borne witness to the enduring friendship between the Chinese and American people. The hope of the China-U.S. relationship lies in the people, its foundation is in our societies, its future depends on the youth, and its vitality comes from exchanges at subnational levels.
(Web editor: Wang Xiaoping, Liang Jun)

item.title: Xi lands in U.S. for state visit, greeted by Trump at airport
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-24
Xi lands in U.S. for state visit, greeted by Trump at airport Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan step out of the airplane cabin upon their arrival at Joint Base Andrews in the United States on Sept. 23, 2026. Xi arrived at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday afternoon for a state visit to the United States at the invitation of U.S. President Donald Trump. Xi and Peng were warmly greeted by Trump and his wife, Melania Trump, at the airport in a rare planeside welcome. (Xinhua/Liu Bin) WASHINGTON, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday afternoon for a state visit to the United States at the invitation of U.S. President Donald Trump. Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, were warmly greeted by Trump and his wife, Melania Trump, at the airport in a rare planeside welcome. American children presented flowers to Xi and Peng. The honor guards lined up on both sides of the red carpet to pay their respects. The welcome ceremony also included a 21-gun salute, the playing of the national anthems of both countries and a military flyover. In a written speech, Xi extended sincere greetings and best wishes to the U.S. people on behalf of the Chinese people. China and the United States are both great countries, and the two peoples are both great peoples, Xi said in the speech, adding that the two peoples have maintained friendly exchanges for a long time and their interests are deeply intertwined. China and the United States should be partners, not rivals, he said, noting that the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand, and that the two countries can help each other succeed and advance the well-being of the whole world. Xi noted that he and Trump agreed to build a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability during Trump's visit to China in May, which has provided strategic guidance for the future development of bilateral ties. China and the United States should work in the same direction, promote a stable relationship featuring cooperation as the mainstay, moderate competition, manageable differences, and promises of peace, Xi said. He said China and the United States, as two major countries, should find a right way to get along in the new era. Xi emphasized that the world is developing and times are changing, but the historical logic of peaceful coexistence between China and the United States has not changed, the goodwill of friendly exchanges between the two peoples has not changed, and the general expectations of the international community for China and the United States have not changed. Xi said he looks forward to having in-depth exchanges with Trump on major issues concerning bilateral relations and the world situation, constantly enriching the connotation of the constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability, and expanding the space for exchanges and cooperation in various fields between the two countries. Xi said he also looks forward to engaging extensively with people from all walks of life in the United States to deepen friendship. With joint efforts, Xi said he believes the visit is sure to be fruitful, and will enhance the well-being of the two peoples and add hope for world peace. On Xi's way from the airport to his hotel by car, representatives of overseas Chinese and students gathered on both sides of the road, waving the national flags of China and the United States to warmly welcome his visit.
